## Social Media Brand Guidelines Checklist for Consistent Content

A social media brand guidelines checklist helps your team publish content that looks, sounds and feels like the same organisation across Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn, YouTube and WhatsApp. It should cover your visual identity, writing style, templates, approval process and platform-specific rules, without making everyday publishing unnecessarily slow.

Consistency does not mean every post has to look identical. It means people should recognise your NGO, school, clinic, D2C brand, agency or local business even when the format changes from a Reel to a LinkedIn post, an Instagram Story or a WhatsApp announcement.

## Why Social Media Brand Guidelines Matter

Many organisations have a logo, a few brand colours and a preferred font. That is a useful starting point, but it is not a complete social media brand system.

A social media presence usually involves several people:

- A founder writing LinkedIn updates
- A designer creating Instagram posts
- A freelancer editing Reels
- A salesperson answering comments
- A staff member sending WhatsApp broadcasts
- An agency scheduling content
- A partner or volunteer creating event announcements

Without clear guidelines, each person makes small decisions independently. One post may use formal language, while another sounds casual. One creative may use the correct logo, while another stretches it or places it over a busy photograph. A school may use one spelling style on Instagram and another on its website. A clinic may publish health-related claims without a consistent review process.

These differences can gradually weaken trust.

For Indian organisations, consistency is also important because audiences often discover a business through multiple channels. Someone may see an Instagram ad, check Google Business Profile, visit the website, read reviews and then ask a question on WhatsApp. If the name, colours, tone and information differ across those touchpoints, the organisation can appear less established than it is.

A practical checklist gives your team a shared reference point. It should answer questions such as:

- Which logo version should be used on a square post?
- What colours are allowed for backgrounds and text?
- Should captions use “you” or “customers”?
- How should prices, GST and offers be written?
- Which claims need approval before publishing?
- How should comments and complaints be handled?
- What should remain consistent across languages?
- Which parts can change for different platforms?

The goal is not to create a large brand manual that nobody opens. The goal is to make correct publishing easier.

## Social Media Brand Guidelines Checklist: The Core Elements

Your checklist should contain both fixed rules and practical examples. Fixed rules protect the brand. Examples help people apply those rules when they are working quickly.

### 1. Brand foundation

Before defining colours and templates, write down the basic identity of the organisation.

Include:

- Official brand name
- Short form or abbreviation, if one is approved
- One-line description of what the organisation does
- Main audience groups
- Key products, services or programmes
- Geographic focus
- Main differentiators
- Brand values
- Primary call to action

For example, a Pune-based clinic may describe itself as a family healthcare clinic serving local residents, while a D2C food brand may focus on convenient products for Indian households. These descriptions influence the language, imagery and content topics you use.

Also define what the brand is not. A low-cost education initiative may not want to sound luxurious. A paediatric clinic may not want to sound overly technical. A social enterprise may want to avoid language that makes beneficiaries sound helpless.

A short foundation section helps content creators make better decisions when a situation is not covered by a specific rule.

### 2. Audience and platform roles

Do not treat every social media platform as if it has the same purpose.

Your guidelines should explain who you are addressing and what each platform is expected to do.

| Platform | Typical role | Content considerations | Common mistake |
|---|---|---|---|
| Instagram | Discovery, visual storytelling and community interaction | Strong first frame, concise captions, Reels, Stories and accessible text | Reusing a poster without adapting it for mobile viewing |
| Facebook | Local community, updates, events and groups | Clear details, location, dates and shareable information | Posting only promotional material |
| LinkedIn | Professional credibility, partnerships and hiring | More context, evidence, founder or team perspective | Using sales-heavy language for every post |
| YouTube | Education, demonstrations and long-form explanation | Thumbnail, title, description and subtitles | Treating a video title like a brochure heading |
| WhatsApp Business | Direct enquiries, support and repeat communication | Permission-based messaging, short updates and clear replies | Sending frequent or irrelevant broadcasts |
| Google Business Profile | Local discovery and trust | Accurate hours, services, photos and updates | Allowing outdated contact details to remain live |

These are general roles, not strict limitations. An NGO may use LinkedIn for partnership updates and Instagram for field stories. A school may use YouTube for parent education and WhatsApp for notices.

The important point is to define the purpose before choosing the format.

### 3. Logo rules

Your social media brand guidelines checklist should include exact logo usage rules.

Specify:

- Approved logo files
- Full-colour, black and white versions
- Minimum size for digital use
- Minimum clear space around the logo
- Approved background colours
- Whether the logo may be placed on photographs
- Whether the symbol can be used without the wordmark
- Rules for profile photos and cover images
- Prohibited modifications

Common logo errors include stretching, rotating, recolouring, adding shadows, placing the logo too close to an edge and using a low-resolution screenshot. These mistakes are easy to avoid when the correct files are stored in a shared folder.

Create separate versions for:

- Profile pictures
- Square posts
- Vertical Stories and Reels
- Landscape banners
- Video end screens
- Website and email use

A circular profile image may crop a horizontal logo. Test the logo in the actual profile-image frame before finalising it.

Do not assume that placing the logo on every creative improves recognition. A small, correctly placed logo is usually better than a large logo that competes with the message.

### 4. Colour palette

List your primary, secondary and supporting colours. Include the colour codes used by designers and developers, such as HEX values for digital work.

Also define:

- Which colours are used for backgrounds
- Which colours are used for headings and body text
- Which colours are reserved for buttons or calls to action
- Which combinations should not be used
- How colour is adapted for dark backgrounds
- Which colours may be used for charts or data
- Whether festive or campaign colours need approval

Colour guidelines should consider readability. Light text on a pale background may look attractive in a design file but become difficult to read on a mobile screen. This matters for older audiences, people with visual impairments and anyone viewing content in bright outdoor conditions.

For Indian brands, seasonal campaigns often introduce new colours. Diwali, Independence Day, regional festivals, school admissions and awareness days may require visual variation. Your guidelines can permit limited campaign colours while keeping the logo, typography and layout recognisable.

### 5. Typography

Choose fonts that are available to the people who will create content. A font that only one designer has licensed may not be practical for a school administrator or NGO coordinator preparing a quick announcement.

Define:

- Primary typeface
- Secondary typeface, if needed
- Heading style
- Body text style
- Number and date formatting
- Font weight rules
- Line spacing
- Text limits for image-based posts
- Devanagari or other Indian-language font choices

If your brand communicates in Marathi, Hindi, Tamil or another Indian language, test the selected fonts with actual words and diacritics. Some typefaces work well in English but appear uneven or crowded in Indian scripts.

Set a hierarchy for content:

- Main headline
- Supporting line
- Detail text
- Call to action
- Legal or mandatory information

Do not use many fonts to make a post look more creative. A clear hierarchy and strong spacing usually create more consistency than decorative typography.

## Visual Identity for Social Media Content

A visual identity is more than a logo and colour palette. It is the repeated pattern of design choices that makes your content recognisable.

### Photography and image selection

Your guidelines should explain what kinds of images represent the brand.

Consider:

- People and settings that should be shown
- Whether images should feel candid or staged
- Lighting preferences
- Composition and cropping
- Use of close-ups, wide shots or product details
- Treatment of staff, students, patients, customers or beneficiaries
- Permission requirements
- Stock image rules
- Image credit requirements

For an NGO, dignity and consent need particular attention. Avoid using images that expose personal information or portray people in a way that reduces them to a problem. Obtain appropriate permission before publishing identifiable photos, especially of children.

For clinics, do not publish patient photographs, medical records or identifiable health information without proper consent. Be cautious with before-and-after imagery and claims that could be interpreted as guaranteed outcomes.

For D2C brands, show products in realistic use. Product images should match what customers will receive, including packaging, size and colour where relevant.

### Illustrations, icons and graphics

Define whether your brand uses line icons, flat illustrations, photography, 3D graphics or a combination.

Specify:

- Illustration style
- Icon stroke or fill style
- Corner radius for cards and shapes
- Use of patterns
- Rules for charts and diagrams
- Whether stock illustrations are allowed
- How cultural or religious symbols may be used

A consistent icon style matters when several posts are viewed together. Mixing cartoon illustrations, corporate stock images and unrelated decorative elements can make the feed look assembled rather than designed.

### Templates

Templates help non-designers create content without starting from a blank page.

Useful templates include:

- Educational carousel
- Customer testimonial, where genuine consent exists
- Event announcement
- Offer or product feature
- Team introduction
- Quote or thought-leadership post
- Reels cover
- Story poll or question
- Recruitment post
- Public notice
- Festival greeting
- Case update or impact story

Each template should have editable areas and locked brand elements. For example, the logo position, footer and typography may be locked, while the headline, photograph and date remain editable.

Do not create only one template for every post. A feed of identical designs may be consistent but difficult to follow. Use a small family of related layouts.

## Tone of Voice and Writing Rules

Visual consistency attracts attention, but verbal consistency builds familiarity. Your tone of voice should guide the words used in captions, replies, videos, website links and WhatsApp messages.

### Define the brand personality

Choose three to five characteristics. Examples include:

- Clear, not complicated
- Warm, not overfamiliar
- Confident, not exaggerated
- Practical, not vague
- Respectful, not paternalistic
- Professional, not stiff
- Encouraging, not pressuring

For each characteristic, give a short example.

Instead of saying “We are innovative and committed to excellence,” a practical brand may say, “We help small organisations manage enquiries, content and customer follow-up from one place.”

The example matters because adjectives can be interpreted differently by different writers.

### Create a do-and-do-not list

Include phrases your brand prefers and phrases it avoids.

For example:

| Prefer | Avoid |
|---|---|
| “Send us a message to discuss your requirement” | “Act now before it is too late” |
| “Designed for small teams” | “The ultimate solution for everyone” |
| “Terms and conditions apply” | Hiding important offer conditions |
| “Learn how the programme works” | “This will change your life” |
| “We are reviewing your question” | “Your complaint is not our responsibility” |

Avoid unsupported superlatives such as “best”, “number one” or “guaranteed” unless the claim is legally and factually supportable.

### Grammar, spelling and punctuation

Decide whether your organisation follows Indian English conventions and document the choice. Include rules for:

- Capitalisation
- Full stops and commas
- Use of abbreviations
- Date format
- Time format
- Rupee notation
- Phone numbers
- Hashtags
- Emojis
- English and regional-language content
- Use of transliterated language

For prices, decide how you will show GST. If a price excludes GST, say so clearly. If an offer has conditions, link to or state those conditions in an accessible way. Avoid making a “limited-time” claim if the duration is not actually defined.

For dates, use a format that cannot be misunderstood. “5 September 2026” is generally clearer than a numeric format that may be read differently.

### Replies, comments and direct messages

Your brand guidelines should cover conversations, not only scheduled posts.

Prepare guidance for:

- Product questions
- Service enquiries
- Complaints
- Refund requests
- Negative reviews
- Spam
- Sensitive subjects
- Political or religious comments
- Requests for medical or legal advice
- Abuse directed at staff
- Questions that require private information

A useful reply framework is:

1. Acknowledge the person’s message.
2. Give the information you can share publicly.
3. Move sensitive details to an approved private channel.
4. State the next step without promising an outcome you cannot control.

For a clinic, public replies should not invite someone to disclose symptoms or medical history in comments. For a school, parent-specific matters should move to an authorised channel. For an NGO, beneficiary information should be handled carefully.

## Content Consistency Across Platforms

The same campaign may appear on several platforms, but it should not be copied without adjustment.

Start with one core message. Then adapt:

- Length
- Format
- Opening line
- Call to action
- Image ratio
- Caption structure
- Link placement
- Subtitles
- Hashtags
- Comment prompts

For example, an event announcement may use a short visual and registration link on Instagram, a detailed explanation on LinkedIn, a local-community post on Facebook and a direct reminder through an opted-in WhatsApp list.

Keep the following details identical wherever they appear:

- Event date and time
- Location
- Registration URL
- Price
- Eligibility
- Contact number
- Product name
- Service inclusions
- Offer validity
- Spelling of the organisation name

A content calendar can support this process. Add fields for the campaign, audience, platform, format, core message, owner, reviewer, publication date, asset link and approval status.

Use a naming convention for files, such as:

`2026-09-school-admissions-instagram-reel-v02`

This makes it easier to identify the latest version and reduces the risk of publishing an outdated creative.

### Accessibility checklist

Accessible content is easier for many people to understand, not only those with disabilities.

Include:

- High contrast between text and background
- Readable font sizes
- Captions on videos
- Alt text where the platform supports it
- Spoken information repeated in captions
- Avoidance of text-heavy graphics
- Clear link labels
- Descriptive thumbnails
- No dependence on colour alone to convey meaning

When creating Marathi, Hindi or other regional-language content, have a fluent reviewer check spelling and meaning. Direct translation can produce language that is technically correct but unnatural for the intended audience.

## Legal, Ethical and Platform Checks in India

Brand guidelines cannot replace legal advice, but they can create a sensible review process.

### Advertising and claims

Promotional content should accurately describe the product or service. Be particularly careful with:

- Health claims
- Educational results
- Financial or investment claims
- Environmental claims
- “Free” offers
- Discounts
- Comparisons with competitors
- Influencer endorsements
- Testimonials
- Before-and-after statements

If a claim depends on conditions, disclose those conditions clearly. Do not use a customer testimonial that has been edited in a way that changes its meaning. Do not create testimonials or reviews that are not genuine.

Influencer and creator collaborations should identify the commercial relationship appropriately. The exact disclosure format may depend on the platform and campaign, so your review process should include a responsible person who checks the current requirements.

### Privacy and consent

Before publishing photos, videos, screenshots or customer messages, confirm:

- Who owns the content
- Whether identifiable people have given permission
- Whether children appear in the content
- Whether personal information is visible
- Whether a phone number, address or email should be removed
- Whether the consent covers social media and paid advertising
- How withdrawal requests will be handled

Screenshots of WhatsApp conversations require particular care. Remove names, numbers, profile photos and sensitive information unless there is a clear and documented reason to publish them.

### GST, pricing and offer details

A social post should not create confusion about whether GST is included. If your business communicates prices, define a consistent format for:

- Inclusive or exclusive GST pricing
- Shipping charges
- Convenience fees
- Subscription billing
- Refund terms
- Offer duration
- Coupon restrictions
- Regional availability

For local businesses, also keep address, service area, operating hours and contact information consistent with Google Business Profile and the website.

## Ownership, Approval and Governance

A checklist is effective only when someone owns each step.

Define the roles involved:

- Content planner
- Writer
- Designer or editor
- Subject-matter reviewer
- Compliance reviewer, where needed
- Final approver
- Publisher
- Community manager

One person may handle several roles in a small organisation. That is acceptable, but the responsibility should still be clear.

### Set approval levels

Not every post needs the same review.

You may use levels such as:

- Routine: regular educational or community content
- Commercial: offers, pricing and product claims
- Sensitive: health, finance, beneficiaries, incidents or complaints
- Urgent: service disruptions, public notices or corrections

Document who approves each level and where approval is recorded. Email, a project-management tool or a dedicated WhatsApp group may be used, but avoid relying on verbal approval that cannot be checked later.

### Create an escalation process

Write down what happens if:

- A post contains an incorrect price
- A customer complains publicly
- An account is hacked
- A staff member publishes from the wrong account
- A copyrighted image is flagged
- A negative review receives attention
- An inaccurate claim has already been published
- A crisis affects the organisation

The process should include who is contacted, who can pause scheduled content and who can issue a correction. Speed is useful, but an unapproved emotional response can create a larger problem.

### Review the guidelines regularly

Review the document when:

- The logo or brand identity changes
- A new product or service launches
- A new platform is added
- The target audience changes
- A regulatory concern arises
- A repeated publishing error is noticed
- The organisation begins using paid advertising
- Multiple agencies or freelancers join the workflow

Keep a version number and review date on the document. Archive old templates so they are not accidentally reused.

## Common Mistakes to Avoid

### Making the document too abstract

Words such as “premium”, “modern” and “friendly” are not enough. Add examples, screenshots and approved templates.

### Creating rules nobody can follow

If the process requires several approvals for a simple event reminder, people may bypass it. Match the process to the risk.

### Treating every platform identically

A square poster copied into a Reel may be unreadable. A long LinkedIn explanation may not work as an Instagram caption. Adapt the execution while protecting the core message.

### Changing brand colours too often

A new colour for every festival, offer or campaign makes the overall identity harder to recognise. Use approved seasonal variations rather than starting from scratch.

### Ignoring non-design content

A brand can look consistent while its replies are inconsistent, dismissive or vague. Include comments, direct messages, calls to action and customer support language.

### Using unverified claims

A designer or social media manager may not know whether a product claim is accurate. Assign subject-matter review for content involving health, education, finance, impact or performance.

### Forgetting regional language quality

Machine translation may produce awkward or misleading content. Use a fluent reviewer who understands the audience and context.

### Failing to update old assets

If your phone number, address, pricing or logo changes, old posts and templates may continue to circulate. Include an asset-audit step in your brand maintenance process.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What should a social media brand guidelines checklist include?

It should include brand foundations, logo rules, colours, typography, photography, templates, tone of voice, grammar, platform roles, accessibility, approval workflows and rules for comments or direct messages. It should also cover consent, privacy, pricing disclosures and content that requires specialist review.

### How long should social media brand guidelines be?

The document should be long enough to answer recurring questions but short enough for the team to use. A compact core guide supported by template examples, approved files and a content checklist is often more practical than a large document that is rarely opened.

### Should every social media post use the same design?

No. Every post should follow the same visual system, but it can use different layouts for education, product information, events, testimonials and video. Repeating the same design for every post may create visual fatigue and make important information harder to notice.

### Can a small business create brand guidelines without an agency?

Yes. Start with the decisions your team makes repeatedly: logo placement, colours, fonts, writing tone, image style, templates and approval rules. An agency or designer can later refine the system, but a simple and consistently used guide is more valuable than an elaborate guide that nobody applies.

### How should NGOs handle photos of beneficiaries on social media?

Use informed, appropriate consent and consider whether publishing the image could expose a person to embarrassment, risk or unwanted attention. Be especially careful with children and sensitive situations, remove unnecessary personal information and avoid language or imagery that takes away people’s dignity.

### How often should social media brand guidelines be updated?

Review them when the brand, audience, platforms, services or publishing team changes. A periodic review can also identify repeated mistakes, outdated contact information and templates that no longer match the organisation’s current communication needs.

## Where to Start

Begin with an audit of your last few weeks of content. Compare profile images, captions, colours, logo use, contact details, prices, calls to action and replies across each active platform.

Then create a working document with these sections:

1. Brand foundation and audience
2. Platform roles
3. Logo, colour and typography rules
4. Image and template guidance
5. Tone of voice and writing examples
6. Accessibility and regional-language checks
7. Consent, privacy and claim review
8. Approval and escalation workflow

Keep approved logos, fonts, templates and sample posts in one shared location. Assign one person to maintain the files and review the checklist when your communication changes.
